interactions.summary: Jiang asks why art betters a person and begins a long classroom probe with the Last Supper, collecting answers about entering the painting, recovering its story, and imaginatively participating in the scene.

claims.claim: Jiang states that the first step of redemption is imagination: art matters because it drives reflective and moral change by expanding the viewer's imaginative capacity.
Jiang treats sustained attention to a painting such as the Last Supper as a transformative exercise: if you sit with the work long enough, it changes you as a person and can make you more virtuous.
The first mechanisms Jiang accepts are participatory and narrative: viewers enter the painting, imagine themselves inside it, and try to fill in the story of the depicted figures.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes an unusually strong thesis claim: if you want to begin redemption, you need imagination first.
signature_moments.source_phrase: If you really want to start the process, you need imagination
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual hinge that links purgatory, art, and moral psychology for the rest of the lecture.

signature_moments.moment: One student describes the right kind of looking as entering the painting and even testing what she would think from Jesus' place at the table.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It concretizes Jiang's participatory model of art rather than leaving imagination abstract.

chronology_notes.note: This packet marks the lecture's major turn from textual exegesis toward a general theory of how art activates imagination and moral formation.
